title.en: Chun Yang on the Swing at Kwanghallu

region.zh: 廣寒樓，南原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Pansori tale set c. 1600s; collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 7 'Chun Yang', eBook #55539

summary.en: In Namwon lived the Prefect's son Ye Toh Ryung, a dutiful scholar of sixteen, who rides out in the first spring weather to Kwang-han Pavilion, the rarest of all views, where the spirits themselves, it is said, frequent the place for its beauty. Leaning on one arm he sees a vision shoot into the air: a beautiful girl swinging in her dooryard — a dazzle of bright silks, shoeless white-stockinged feet shooting up among the peach blossoms till her hairpin falls and breaks with a sharp click. She is Chun Yang Ye, Fragrant Spring, daughter of Uhl Mah the dancing girl. The servant is sent running; brought before the young man, she matches him in age — twice eight and four fours — born at midnight of the eighth of the fourth moon, the lantern festival, one hour later than his own. 'Surely the gods had some motive in sending us into the world at the same time,' he says, and pleads that heaven must have intended them man and wife.
summary.zh: 南原使君之子李夢龍，春日遊廣寒樓。方倚欄看山，忽見鄰院少女蕩鞦韆直上雲際，羅衣生風，繡履掠桃，釵墮而折。急問之，乃歌伎月梅之女成春香也。召至，同年同月同日生，惟相差一時辰。夢龍曰：『此天作之合也。』遂求婚。

sensitivity.note: Pansori classic Chunhyang; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the city of Nam Won, in Chull Lah Do, lived the Prefect Ye Tung Uhi, the happy father of a son of some sixteen years of age, a bright, quick-minded, dutiful boy. As the mild spring weather approached and the buds began to open to the singing of the joyful birds, Ye Toh Ryung felt that he must get out and enjoy nature, and asked his pang san concerning the neighboring views. 'But of all rare views, Kang Hal Loo is the rarest,' said the servant. 'Officers from the eight provinces come to enjoy the scenery, and the temple is covered with verses they have left in praise of the place.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'That is true; so true, in fact, that it is well known that the spirits do frequent this place for its beauty.' As he said this, Toh Ryung had raised himself, gazing out to one side, when, as though it were one of the spirits just mentioned, the vision of a beautiful girl shot up into the air and soon fell back out of sight in the shrubbery of an adjoining court-yard. The vision arose again, and he then had time to see that it was but a beautiful girl swinging in her dooryard — the jewels sparkling on the gay robes, the dainty white hands and full round arms, and, as she flew higher in her wild sport, two little shoeless feet encased in white stockings shot up among the peach blossoms, causing them to fall in showers all about her. In the midst of the sport her hairpin loosened and fell, allowing her raven locks to float about her shoulders; the costly ornament fell on a rock and broke, for Toh Ryung could hear the sharp click where he sat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'She is Uhl Mahs' daughter, a gee sang of this city; her name is Chun Yang Ye — fragrant spring.' The servant ran and called her. 'What is your name?' asked he. 'My name is Chun Yang Ye,' she said, with a voice that resembled silver jingling in a pouch. 'How old are you?' 'My age is just twice eight years.' 'Ah ha! how fortunate; you are twice eight, and I am four fours. We are of the same age. Your name, Fragrant Spring, is the same as your face — very beautiful.' 'My birthday occurs at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth moon.' 'That is the date of the lantern festival, and it is also my own birthday, only I was born at eleven instead of twelve. Surely the gods had some motive in sending us into the world at the same time, and thus bringing us together at our sixteenth spring-tide. Heaven must have intended us to be man and wife.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Written Contract for a Hundred Years

region.zh: 廣寒樓，南原（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Pansori tale set c. 1600s; collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 7, eBook #55539

summary.en: Toh Ryung begs Chun Yang to marry him, but she is no silly foolish thing: 'The son of a nobleman may not marry a gee sang without the consent of his parents... should we be privately married, and your father be ordered to duty at some other place, you would not dare take me with you. Then you would marry the daughter of some nobleman, and I would be forgotten.' He swears a yangban has but one mouth and cannot speak two ways; she answers that words fly out of the mouth and are soon lost — ink and paper are more lasting. Instantly he writes: 'Desiring to enjoy the spring scenery, I came to Kang Hal Loo. There I saw for the first time my heaven-sent bride. Meeting for the first time, I pledge myself for one hundred years; to be her faithful husband. Should I change, show this paper to the magistrate.' That night, scaling the back wall after his father sleeps, he comes to her house with its banner praying that a century be short to span her life and happiness; over the wine she sings that the flowers can bloom but a few days at best, and they pledge that when death should overtake them she will enter a flower, while he becomes a butterfly, coming and resting on her bosom and feasting off her fragrant sweetness.
summary.zh: 夢龍欲娶，春香曰：『貴公子不得私娶伎女；且異日尊翁遷任，君必不能攜我，則娶高門而棄我矣。』夢龍誓之，春香曰：『言出無憑，立券為信。』夢龍即書券曰：『遊廣寒樓，始遇天配之妻，百年偕老；若負此心，持券告官。』夜逾牆而至其家，酒酣對酌，相誓曰：『他日我為蝶，汝為花，蝶常棲花懷而餐其香。』

passages.text: 'You know,' she said, 'the son of a nobleman may not marry a gee sang without the consent of his parents. I know I am a gee sang by name, the fates have so ordained, but, nevertheless, I am an honorable woman, always have been, and expect to remain so.' 'Certainly, we cannot celebrate the six customs ceremony, but we can be privately married just the same.' 'No, it cannot be. Your father would not consent, and should we be privately married, and your father be ordered to duty at some other place, you would not dare take me with you. Then you would marry the daughter of some nobleman, and I would be forgotten. It must not, cannot be.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I will never forsake you, or marry another. I swear it. And a yang ban has but one mouth, he cannot speak two ways. Even should we leave this place I will take you with me, or return soon to you.' 'But suppose you change your mind or forget your promises; words fly out of the mouth and are soon lost, ink and paper are more lasting; give me your promises in writing,' she says. Instantly the young man took up paper and brush, and wrote: 'A memorandum. Desiring to enjoy the spring scenery, I came to Kang Hal Loo. There I saw for the first time my heaven-sent bride. Meeting for the first time, I pledge myself for one hundred years; to be her faithful husband. Should I change, show this paper to the magistrate.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the lights were extinguished and his father had gone to sleep, he took his trusty servant, and, scaling the back wall, they hurried to the house of Chun Yang Ye. On the door leading to her little parlor hung a banner inscribed with verses to her ancestors and descendants, praying that a century be short to span her life and happiness. Pouring out a cup, she sang to him: 'This is the elixir of youth; drinking this, may you never grow old; though ten thousand years pass over your head, may you stand like the mountain that never changes.' They pledged themselves anew; not content with promises for this short life, they went into the future, and he yielded readily to her request, that when death should at last o'ertake them, she would enter a flower, while he would become a butterfly, coming and resting on her bosom, and feasting off her fragrant sweetness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Broken Mirror and the Grand Examination

region.en: Namwon prison and Seoul examination grounds (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南原監獄與漢京試場（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Pansori tale set c. 1600s; collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 7, eBook #55539

summary.en: Promoted to Secretary of Finance, the father must move to Seoul; Chun Yang despairs — 'If we say good-by, it will be forever' — and is given his crystal mirror as pledge, giving him her jade ring in turn: 'My love, like this ring, knows no end... take your books, study hard, and enter the examinations.' She removes her own name from the district register of dancing girls, for she is now a married woman. In Namwon a new magistrate arrives, a hard-faced politician resolved to marry the matchless beauty; when she refuses — 'A thousand deaths first' — she is chained and thrown into prison, wearing at last the huge neck-encircling cangue. One night she dreams her gift-mirror breaks in halves; a blind fortune-teller interprets: the bird that flew in as it broke was a bearer of good news concerning Toh Ryung, and the sticks, thrown and chanted, answer that he has passed his examinations, been promoted, and will soon come to her. In Seoul, Toh Ryung takes the grand guaga on the subject 'A lad playing in the shade of a pine tree is questioned by an aged wayfarer' and wins first honors; he asks to be made a Ussa, government inspector, and rides south disguised as a beggar.
summary.zh: 李父升戶曹參判，攜眷赴京。春香大慟，夢龍以水晶鏡為信，春香以玉釧贈之曰：『吾心如釧，無有終已。入京後當勤學應試。』自除樂籍。新任使君聞春香之美，欲妻之；春香拒曰『寧死不從』，遂荷枷下獄。夜夢鏡碎，延瞽者占之，曰『碎鏡有聲，又有鳥入，主好音至；夫君登第，不日當歸』。夢龍果於京師大比奪魁，乞為暗察使，微服南下。

sensitivity.note: Pansori classic; magistrate coercion depicted at summary level.

passages.text: 'Oh, how can we separate. We must die, we cannot live apart... If we say good-by, it will be forever; we can never meet again.' 'Don't cry so bitterly; we have contracted for one hundred years, and this will be but a bitter separation that will make our speedy reunion more blissful. Here, take this crystal mirror as a pledge that I will keep my word.' Taking off her jade ring, she gave it to him for a keepsake, saying: 'My love, like this ring, knows no end... If you go to Seoul, you must not trifle, but take your books, study hard, and enter the examinations, then, perhaps, you may obtain rank and come to me. I will stand with my hand shading my eyes, ever watching for your return.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: A new magistrate came to Nam Won, a hard-faced, hard-hearted politician who devoted himself to riotous living. He had not been long in the place till he had heard so much of the matchless beauty of Chun Yang Ye that he determined to see, and if, as reported, marry her. 'A nobleman's son cannot really marry a dancing girl,' yelled the enraged officer; she answered, 'Though born a gee sang, I am by marriage a lady,' and then, 'Never. A thousand deaths first.' The man was beside himself with wrath, and ordered her chained and thrown into prison at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: One night she dreamed that she was in her own room, dressing, and using the little mirror Toh Ryung had given her, when it suddenly broke in halves. Pondering much upon the dream, she called the jailer and asked him to summon a blind man, as she wished her fortune told. 'The bird was bearer of good news, and the breaking of the mirror, which Toh Ryung gave you, indicates that the news concerned him,' said the old man, arranging a bunch of sticks and throwing them upon the floor: 'Your husband has done well. He has passed his examinations, been promoted, and will soon come to you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the meantime Ye Toh Ryung had continued his studious work day and night. A royal proclamation announced a grand guaga, and Ye Toh Ryung was given as a subject for his composition, 'A lad playing in the shade of a pine tree is questioned by an aged wayfarer.' The composition rolled forth as though he had committed it from the ancient classics, and before any other papers were received it was known that none could excel this one. The King gave him the three glasses of wine, a wreath of flowers from his own hands, and the court hat with lateral wings denoting the rapidity with which he must execute his Sovereign's commands; and Ye Toh Ryung asked for the arduous duties of Ussa, government inspector, and set out disguised as a beggar for his former home in the southern province.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Beggar at the Magistrate's Birthday Feast

texts.period: Pansori tale set c. 1600s; collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 7, eBook #55539

summary.en: Disguised as a beggar, the Ussa hears from farmers that the Prefect extorts rice and money unjustly and has imprisoned the fair Chun Yang Ye because she repulsed him. Arriving on the day of the Magistrate's birthday feast — wine to flow like water, dancing girls from the whole district — he breaks into the court, is humored with scraps, demands his own singing girl, and then, 'in return for your food and wine,' writes verses: 'The oil that enriches the food of the official is but the life blood of the down-trodden people, whose tears are of no more merit in the eyes of the oppressor than the drippings of a burning candle.' A troubled look passes over all; the host orders him cast into prison, but the Ussa takes out his official seal: terror blanches the half-drunken faces, the wicked host is caught trying to crawl under the house and bound with chains. Chun Yang is carried in shackled to answer charges — until he asks her in his own voice to glance at him, and she faints in the attempt to run; the mother dashes away her dishes and tears around for joy: 'What a delightful birthday surprise for a cruel magistrate!' The marriage was publicly solemnized at Seoul, and the Ussa was raised to a high position, while the country rang with the praises of his faithful wife.
summary.zh: 暗察使微服乞食，聞野老言使君暴斂，又繫春香於獄。會使君壽誕大宴，乞兒突入，索酒索歌，乃題詩於紙曰：『使君之膏粱，乃百姓之膏血；民之涕淚，於虎吏直燭淚耳。』滿座失色。使君怒命下獄，乞兒出御賜印信，眾皆股慄，使君方鑽床底而被縛。春香被械至，忽聞其聲，見其人，大呼奔抱而暈。老嫗聞訊，棄盂而舞曰：『好一個生辰之賀禮！』後夫婦入京完婚，春香之賢，天下傳頌。

sensitivity.note: Pansori classic; official corruption exposed; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: A band of farmers were plowing with lazy bulls, singing a grateful song in praise of their just King. The Ussa came along in his disguise and began to jest with them, and an old man cautioned the rest: 'Don't you see, this man's speech is only half made up of our common talk; he is playing a part. I think he must be a gentleman in disguise.' Questioned concerning the Prefect, the old man answered, 'His heart is as hard and unbending as the dead heart of the ancient oak. He extorts rice and money unjustly, and spends his ill-gotten gains in riotous living. He has imprisoned and beaten the fair Chun Yang Ye because she repulsed him, and she now lies near to death in the prison.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The attendants informed him that the next day was the birthday of the Magistrate, that a great feast was to take place in the morning when wine would flow like water, with the gee sang from the whole district performing. The disguised Ussa presented himself at the yamen gate, where the servants jeered at him; he climbed through a break in the wall and again presented himself before the feasters. 'I am a beggar, give me food and drink that I, too, may enjoy myself' — and when each guest had a fair gee sang to sing a wine song while they drank, he claimed the same: the girl sang him a song that wished him speedy death instead of long life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I thank you for your food and wine and the graciousness of my reception; in return for which I will amuse you by writing you some verses,' he said, and wrote: 'The oil that enriches the food of the official is but the life blood of the down-trodden people, whose tears are of no more merit in the eyes of the oppressor than the drippings of a burning candle.' When this was read, a troubled look passed over all. The host laughed and ordered attendants to take the intruder and cast him into prison for his impudence — but the Ussa took out his official seal, giving the preconcerted signal that summoned his ready followers. At sight of the King's seal terror blanched the faces of each of the half-drunken men; the wicked host tried to crawl under the house and escape, but was caught and bound with chains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: A chair was sent for Chun Yang Ye, whose servants bore her to the yamen, where the Ussa addressed her in a changed voice, commanding her to look up and answer her charges. Failing in this way, he then asked her in his own voice to just glance at him. Surprised, she looked up, and her dazed eyes saw her lover standing there in his proper guise; with a delighted cry she tried to run to him but fainted in the attempt, and was borne in his arms to a room. The old mother, dashing away her dishes, tore around for joy, crying, 'What a delightful birthday surprise for a cruel magistrate!' The marriage was publicly solemnized at Seoul, and the Ussa was raised to a high position, in which he was just to the people, who loved him for his virtues, while the country rang with the praises of his faithful wife, who became the mother of many children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 7 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Sim Chung Born of a Star

texts.period: Pansori tale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 8 'Sim Chung', eBook #55539

summary.en: Sim Hyun, a gentleman scholar, and his beautiful accomplished wife wait fifteen years for a child, till the wife dreams a brilliant dream in which a star comes down to her from the skies — and a child is given, a girl. The child's cheeks are full-blown roses; her father, whose feeble eyes refuse their office, keeps her continually by his side to guide his footsteps. When the mother dies the father emerges totally blind; in ten years they have used up the homestead, and the blind man falls into a deep ditch, where a voice tells him: 'True, you are blind, yet not incurably so. I am the old priest of the temple in the mountain fortress... In case you make an offering of three hundred bags of rice to the Buddha of our temple, you will be restored to sight, you will be given rank and dignity, while your daughter will become the first woman in all Korea.' He signs the order in pencil and paper and takes to pounding rice in the stone mortars; when the priest comes for his pay, the daughter, after her midnight bath and a dream in which her mother comes down from heaven to comfort her, resolves to sell herself.
summary.zh: 沈學官夫婦祈子十五年，妻夢星墜而孕，生女沉清，貌若朝霞。未幾母歿，父喪明，家產蕩盡。盲翁墮溝，遇山寺老僧曰：『施米三百石於佛前，則目當復明，貴及子孫。』盲翁立券。僧催債，沉清沐浴禱天，夢母自天降而慰之，遂決意鬻身。

sensitivity.note: Pansori classic Sim Cheong; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Sim Hyun was highly esteemed in the Korean village in which he resided; he belonged to the Yang Ban, or gentleman class. After fifteen years of childless waiting, the wife of Sim dreamed again; this time her vision was a brilliant one, and in it she saw a star come down to her from the skies above. She was right: a child was given to them, but, to their great dismay, it was only a girl. Heaven had kindly prepared the way for the little visitor, however, for after fifteen years weary waiting, they were not going to look with serious disfavor upon a girl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: At three years of age she bade fair to far surpass her mother's noted beauty and accomplishments; her cheeks were full-blown roses. The father forgot that his offspring was not a boy, and had his child continually by his side to guide his footsteps, as his feeble eyes refused to perform their office. Just as their joy seemed too great to be lasting, it was suddenly checked by the death of the mother, which plunged them into a deep grief from which the father emerged totally blind. Little by little household trinkets were given to the brokers, and in ten years they had used up the homestead and all it contained.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day in his journeying the blind man fell into a deep ditch, from which he could not extricate himself. 'I am blind, not drunk,' he called out, and the passing stranger answered: 'I know full well you are not drunk. True, you are blind, yet not incurably so. I am the old priest of the temple in the mountain fortress. I am a prophet, and I have had a vision concerning you. In case you make an offering of three hundred bags of rice to the Buddha of our temple, you will be restored to sight, you will be given rank and dignity, while your daughter will become the first woman in all Korea.' 'You may give me your order for it, and pay it along as you are able' — and the blind man gave his order for the costly price of his sight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: One night, as the dinner was spread, the priest came and demanded his pay; the old blind man lost his appetite and had to explain the compact to his daughter. That night, after her midnight bath, she lay down on a mat in the open air and gazed up to heaven, praying that her poor father might be restored to health and sight; she fell asleep and dreamed that her mother came down from heaven to comfort her, and told her not to worry, that a means would be found for the payment of the rice, and that soon all would be happy again in the little family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

region.en: Indangsu, the evil spirit's waters (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Pansori tale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 8, eBook #55539

summary.en: A great merchant sailing to China is distressed by an evil spirit in the waters he must pass; priests have told him the sacrifice of a young maiden would quiet it, and he offers a great sum. Sim Chung, hearing of it, decides it must be the fulfilment of her dream: she puts on old clothes, fasts on the journey to look wan and haggard like one in mourning, and tells her father she is going to bow at her mother's grave. The merchant's overseer is struck by her dignity: 'Ah! now I see the true nobility of your character. I did not know that such filial piety existed outside the works of the ancients.' Three hundred bags of rice go to the priest in a procession of one hundred and fifty ponies; her doom fixed, she prays: 'I am only fourteen years old, and have but four more hours to live. What will become of my poor father?' A stranger on a donkey leaves her a cheque of fifty bags of rice for his support; she takes a last farewell and leaves her fainting father to go to her bed in the sea. Dressed in bridal garments at the head of a procession of boats, she prays to heaven, bides them all good-by, and leaps into the sea; above, all is quiet, the waves subside, the sea becomes like a lake, and the boats pass on unmolested.
summary.zh: 海商過印塘水，為水怪所祟，須以處女祭之。沉清自請以身相代，易緇衣而往。三百石米既施，其命已定，乃泣曰：『兒年十四，命在須臾，父其誰養？』有驢上過客遺五十石米券而去。至期，舟列成行，沉清著嫁衣，拜別眾人，躍入海中。風浪頓息，海平如鏡，舟行無恙。

sensitivity.note: Pansori classic; human sacrifice motif handled at summary level.

passages.text: The next day she chanced to hear of the wants of a great merchant who sailed in his large boats to China for trade, but was greatly distressed by an evil spirit that lived in the water through which he must pass. Priests had told him that the sacrifice of a young maiden to the spirit would quiet it and remove the trouble; he was anxious to find the proper person, and had offered a great sum to obtain such an one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sim Chung, hearing of this, decided that it must be the fulfilment of her dream, and having determined to go and offer herself, she put on old clothes and fasted while journeying, that she might look wan and haggard, like one in mourning. When the merchant saw the applicant he was at once struck with her beauty and dignity of carriage; she told her story and said she would give herself for the three hundred bags of rice. 'Ah! now I see the true nobility of your character. I did not know that such filial piety existed outside the works of the ancients,' said the man, who happened to be but an overseer for a greater merchant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: She got the rice and took it to the priest in a long procession of one hundred and fifty ponies; the debt cancelled and her doom fixed, she prayed to heaven, saying: 'I am only fourteen years old, and have but four more hours to live. What will become of my poor father? Kind heaven, protect him when I am gone.' While the wailing and heart-breaking was going on, a stranger rode up on a donkey and comforted the girl by giving her a cheque for fifty bags of rice for the support of the father when his daughter should be no more. She took it gratefully, gave it to the neighbors to keep in trust, prepared herself, took a last farewell, and left her fainting father to go to her bed in the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: In due time the boat that bore Sim Chung, at the head of a procession of boats, arrived at the place where the evil spirit reigned. She was dressed in bridal garments furnished by the merchant. The kind merchant tried once more to appease the spirit by an offering of eatables, but it was useless; whereupon Sim Chung prayed to heaven, bade them all good-by, and leaped into the sea. Above, all was quiet, the waves subsided, the sea became like a lake, and the boats passed on their way unmolested.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sea King Reveals the Star

region.en: Palace of the Sea King (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Pansori tale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 8, eBook #55539

summary.en: When Sim Chung regains her consciousness she is seated in a little boat drawn by fishes, pretty maidens giving her drink from a carved jade bottle: 'We are servants of the King of the Sea, and we are taking you to his palace.' She passes forests of waving plants to a palace whose massive walls are of precious stones, pearls covering the heads of the nails in the great doors, the walks of polished black marble, the light through the water forming beautifully colored clouds. Borne before the King, she protests she is but the daughter of a beggar; the King smiles: 'I know more of you than you know of yourself. You were once a star... you abused your office as cup-bearer to the King of Heaven, and let your lover have free access to all of the choice wines of the palace; as punishment you were banished to earth — sent your lover first, and after keeping you in prison for a long time, sent as daughter to your former lover. He is the man you claim as father. Heaven has seen your filial piety, however, and repents.'
summary.zh: 沉清醒時已坐於群魚曳引之小舟，龍宮侍女以玉瓶進漿。至海龍王之殿，寶石為牆，珠為釘飾，黑玉為階，光影成霞。王曰：『汝前世乃天星也，因私以天酒飲所歡，被謫人間。先遣其人下界，汝則繫於幽獄多時，始降為其女——即今之盲翁是也。上天鑒爾孝心，悔前譴，當厚報之。』

passages.text: When Sim Chung regained her consciousness she was seated in a little boat drawn by fishes, and pretty maidens were giving her to drink from a carved jade bottle. 'We are servants of the King of the Sea, and we are taking you to his palace.' They passed through forests of waving plants, and saw great lazy fish feeding about in the water, till at last they reached the confines of the palace: the massive walls were composed of precious stones, pearls covered the heads of the nails in the great doors, the walks were of polished black marble that shone in the water, and the light, as it passed through the water, formed most beautifully colored clouds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: A mighty noise was heard, and the King passed by preceded by an army with gayly colored satin banners, each bearer blowing on an enormous shell, borne in a golden chair on the shoulders of one hundred men, followed by musicians and dancing girls. The King treated her with great respect, and she protested that she was but the daughter of a beggar, for whom she thought she was giving her life when rescued by these maidens.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The King smiled a little, and said: 'Ah! I know more of you than you know of yourself. You must know that I am the Sea King, and that we know full well the doings of the stars which shine in the heaven above, for they continually visit us on light evenings. Well, you were once a star. You favored one star more than the others, and, in your attentions to him, you abused your office as cup-bearer to the King of Heaven, and let your lover have free access to all of the choice wines of the palace. As punishment, the King decided to banish you to earth; he sent your lover first, and after keeping you in prison for a long time, sent you as daughter to your former lover. He is the man you claim as father. Heaven has seen your filial piety, however, and repents. You will be hereafter most highly favored, as a reward for your dutiful conduct.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Flower in the Glass House and the Scales Falling Away

texts.period: Pansori tale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 8, eBook #55539

summary.en: When the time comes for her departure, a large and beautiful flower is brought into her chamber, so arranged that Sim Chung can conceal herself inside, nourished by its perfume and juice; floated to the surface, it is secured by her friend the merchant and presented to the King, who keeps it in a glass house and never tires of watching. One restless night the King sees her walking in the moonlight before she can hide; the flower vanishes, leaving her standing alone, and she calms his fear: she is but a human being. An officer versed in astronomy reports a brilliant star descended from heaven and alighted upon the palace; the queen being deceased, the King takes the remarkable maiden for his wife in the royal wedding hall. Loneliness for her father moves the Queen to summon all the blind men of the country to a feast of clothing, food and cash; on the third day a feeble old man in rags comes tottering up, and at her pavilion she screams, 'My father! my father!' and falls at his feet senseless. 'Oh! my child, can the dead come back to us? I hear your voice; I feel your form; but how can I know it is you, for I have no eyes? Away with these sightless orbs!' — and tearing at his eyes with his nails, the scales fall away, and he stands rejoicing in his sight once more. The King makes the old man an officer of high rank, appoints him a fine house, and marries him to the accomplished daughter of an officer of suitable rank, fulfilling the last of the prophecy of both the aged priest and the King of the Sea.
summary.zh: 龍王以神花浮送沉清還陽，商得之獻於王，王置之琉璃亭，旦夕玩賞。一夕王見花中步出美人，遂冊立為后。后思父，乃下詔集天下盲人賜宴三日。第三日有一襤褸老人扶杖至，后一見呼曰『父也』，暈於其前。翁曰『吾目已盲，安知汝為吾女』，以手自抉其目，瞖膜忽落，目光頓復。王授翁以高官，聘名門之女妻之，果如老僧與龍王所預言。

sensitivity.note: Pansori classic; restoration-of-sight miracle; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: When the proper time arrived for her departure for the world she had left, a large and beautiful flower was brought into her chamber, so arranged that Sim Chung could conceal herself inside of it, while the delicious perfume and the juice of the plant were ample nourishment. The flower was conveyed to the surface of the sea, at the place where she had plunged in; the merchant steering close managed to secure the flower and place it safely in his boat, deciding at once to present it at the palace if he could get it there. The plan succeeded, and His Majesty, delighted with the gift, spent his time gazing upon it to the exclusion of state business.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: At night, when all was quiet, Sim Chung was wont to come forth and rest herself by walking in the moonlight; the King, being indisposed, went to breathe the rich perfume and chanced to see her before she could conceal herself. She took refuge in her flower, when, to the amazement of both, the flower vanished, leaving her standing alone; she called to him not to fear, that she was but a human being, and no spirit. An officer versed in astronomy stated that on the previous night they had observed a brilliant star descend from heaven and alight upon the palace, boding good to the royal family; the queen being deceased, it was soon decided that the King should take this remarkable maiden for his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sim Chung became lonely and mourned for her poor father; she was oppressed by a strange dream concerning a poor blind man, and was desirous of alleviating in some way the sufferings of the many blind men in the country. Together they agreed to summon all the blind men of the country to a great feast, at which they should be properly clothed, amply fed, and treated each to a present of cash. The Queen secreted herself in a pavilion; she watched the first day and the second in vain, when, as the feast was closing on the third day, a feeble old man in rags came tottering up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her Majesty scrutinized him closely, and then screamed, 'My father! my father!' and fell at his feet senseless. As the full truth began to dawn upon the poor old blind man, he cried: 'Oh! my child, can the dead come back to us? I hear your voice; I feel your form; but how can I know it is you, for I have no eyes? Away with these sightless orbs!' And he tore at his eyes with his nails, when to his utter amazement and joy the scales fell away, and he stood rejoicing in his sight once more. His Majesty made the old man an officer of high rank, appointed him a fine house, and had him married to the accomplished daughter of an officer of suitable rank, thereby fulfilling the last of the prophecy of both the aged priest and the King of the Sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 8 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Hong Kil Tong and the Dragon in the Dream

texts.period: Novel tale (c. 1600s) collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 9 'Hong Kil Tong', eBook #55539

summary.en: Hong Pansa, a noble of high rank, dreams he hears the noise of thunder and sees a huge dragon entering his apartment, too small to contain the enormous body; he takes it as a good omen of a blessing, hoping another son. Within the year a son of marvellous beauty is born to a concubine from the dancing girls — much to the annoyance of his wife — and is named Hong Kil Tong. The boy learns rapidly and surprises every one by his remarkable ability; he rebels at being placed with the slaves and at not being allowed to call his parent father. 'Heaven has made all things for the use of men,' he tells his father in the moonlit courtyard, 'and the laws of men are only made to assist a few; but I am not inclined to submit to any such tyranny, but will become a great man in spite of my evil surroundings.' 'What a pity that he is not my proper and legitimate son,' muses the father. 'As it is, I fear he will cause me serious trouble.'
summary.zh: 洪參判夢雷聲大作，巨龍入室，身大而室小不能容。以為吉兆，果妾生子，貌極美，名洪吉童。吉童穎悟絕倫，而以庶出不得稱父，憤曰：『天生萬物以養人，人法乃護少數人者；吾終不受此縛，必為人上人。』父歎曰：『此兒非常人，惜非嫡子，恐為吾家之禍。』

sensitivity.note: Robin-Hood hero of the first Korean vernacular novel; class discrimination theme.

passages.text: During the reign of the third king in Korea there lived a noble of high rank and noted family, by name Hong. When Hong Pansa was the father of but two sons, he dreamed by night on one occasion that he heard the noise of thunder, and looking up he saw a huge dragon entering his apartment, which seemed too small to contain the whole of his enormous body. The dream was so startling as to awaken the sleeper, who at once saw that it was a good omen, a token of a blessing about to be conferred.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Within the year, however, a son of marvellous beauty was born to one concubine, much to the annoyance of his wife, for he would have been glad to have the beautiful boy a full son, and eligible to office. The child was named Kil Tong. He grew fast, and became more and more beautiful; he learned rapidly, and surprised every one by his remarkable ability. As he grew up he rebelled at being placed with the slaves, and at not being allowed to call his parent, father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: One bright moonlight night Hong Pansa saw his son in the court-yard practising the arts of the soldier, and asked him what it meant. Kil Tong answered that he was fitting himself to become a man that people should respect and fear. 'I know that heaven has made all things for the use of men, if they found themselves capable of using them, and that the laws of men were only made to assist a few that could not otherwise do as they would; but I am not inclined to submit to any such tyranny, but will become a great man in spite of my evil surroundings.' 'This is a most remarkable boy,' mused Hong Pansa. 'What a pity that he is not my proper and legitimate son, that he might be an honor to my name. As it is, I fear he will cause me serious trouble.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fortune-Teller's Prophecy and the Escape from the Assassins

region.en: Hong mansion and mountain storm (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 洪府與荒山（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Novel tale (c. 1600s) collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 9, eBook #55539

summary.en: The jealous wife and concubine hire sorceresses, who send an old woman from the east gate to 'foretell' the boy's future: 'This will be a very great man; if not a king, he will be greater than the king, and will avenge his early wrongs by killing all his family.' The father locks Kil Tong in a strong room; the concubine finally persuades him to send assassins, while a spirit fills the father with disease and the mootang drum and dance in vain. Musing in the dark on the unjust laws that allow sons to be born of concubines but deny them rights, Kil Tong hears a crow caw three times — 'This means something ill to me' — and the window opens on the assassins, who find the room empty and wound each other, killing the old woman their guide; the room has disappeared, they are surrounded by high mountains in a mighty storm with rocks flying through the air, until music sounds and a boy comes riding by on a donkey playing a flute: Kil Tong, who takes their weapons and spares them on condition they never try to kill another man. He cures his father with medicine in a night visit, bades his mother good-by, and starts for an unknown country.
summary.zh: 嫡母與妖妾賄巫嫗，誣吉童他日必弒全家。父乃禁之密室，尋命刺客殺之。吉童夜聞烏鴉三噪，自知有變；刺客入室，空無一人，反自相殘殺，並斃其導者嫗。忽大風起，飛沙走石，四山合圍。忽聞笛聲，見一童騎驢吹笛而至，即吉童也，奪其兵刃，誓不許再殺人乃貸其死。吉童以藥起父疾，別母而遁。

sensitivity.note: Assassination attempt depicted at summary level.

passages.text: The wife of Hong Pansa and his other concubine, seeing how much their lord and master thought of Kil Tong, grew to hate the latter intensely, and called some mootang, or sorceresses, who sent the old woman who lives by the east gate. Kil Tong came as called, and on seeing him the hag bowed and said: 'Send out all of the people. This will be a very great man; if not a king, he will be greater than the king, and will avenge his early wrongs by killing all his family.' At this the father called to her to stop, and enjoined strict secrecy upon her; he sent Kil Tong at once to a strong room and had him locked in for safe keeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The unnatural father was kept in continual excitement by his wicked concubine, and was finally persuaded to send for the assassins. But a spirit filled the father with disease, and he told the men to stay their work; the mootang women were called in, and they beat their drums and danced about the room conjuring the spirit to leave, but it would not obey — till they said, at the suggestion of the concubine, that Kil Tong was the cause of the disorder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: While thus musing in the darkness of the night, he heard a crow caw three times and fly away. 'This means something ill to me,' thought he; and just then his window was thrown open, and in stepped the assassins. They made at the boy, but he was not there; in their rage they wounded each other and killed the old woman who was their guide. To their amazement the room had disappeared, and they were surrounded by high mountains; a mighty storm arose, and rocks flew through the air. Music was heard, and a boy came riding by on a donkey, playing a flute: he took away their weapons, showed himself to be Kil Tong, and promised not to kill them on condition that they should never try to kill another man — for he would know if the promise was broken.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kil Tong went by night to see his father, who thought him a spirit and was very much afraid. He gave his father medicine, which instantly cured him; and sending for his mother, bade her good-by, and started for an unknown country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Stone Door of the Robber Stronghold

region.en: Barren peak in the southern mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南方高山絕頂（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Novel tale (c. 1600s) collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 9, eBook #55539

summary.en: Free at last, Kil Tong journeys south, ascends the lonely mountains where tigers abound yet molest him not, and finds high on a barren peak a huge stone door in the bare wall of rock. Opening it he steps into an open plain surrounded by inaccessible mountains, with over two hundred good houses and many men. 'We are called thieves; but we only despoil the hated official class of some of their ill-gotten gains. No man can enter our stronghold and depart alive, unless he has become one of us; and he must prove himself strong in body and mind.' Kil Tong chooses his own trial: going up to a huge rock on which several men are seated, he lays hold of it and hurls it to some distance. He is installed a member, the contract sealed by mingling blood from the lips of all the members, and made chief. For their first great raid he disguises himself in the red gown of a betrothed youth, presents a forged letter and a promised train of one hundred ponies loaded with rice to the rich, licentious temple priests — and when the ponies arrive, the 'grooms' hiding robbers seize the servants while the priests are bent in humiliation over a pebble produced from the guest's mouth. The band loads the ponies with jewels, rice and cash, and escapes by the main road while Kil Tong, disguised as a priest, leads the belated soldiers down a by-path in the wrong direction.
summary.zh: 吉童遁入深山，見石壁上有巨門一扇，啟之則別有天地，屋舍二百餘，盜眾聚焉。眾曰：『吾儕所劫者贓官耳。入吾山者非入夥即死，且須力試。』吉童舉巨石而擲之，眾驚服，歃血為盟，推為首領。吉童乃扮紅衣新郎，偽稱洪參判之子，齎父書並百匹載米之駝隊往巨刹布施；寺僧大喜，設宴。吉童忽自口中吐石一粒，曰『以此待客耶』，僧慚俯首。伏兵齊起，盡縛僧眾，載其金寶而去；吉童又扮僧引官兵於歧路。眾益神之。

sensitivity.note: Social-bandit romance; anti-elite satire; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Kil Tong, free at last, journeyed to the south, and began to ascend the lonely mountains. Tigers were abundant, but he feared them not, and they seemed to avoid molesting him. After many days he found himself high up on a barren peak enveloped by the clouds. Through the clouds at some distance he espied a huge stone door in the bare wall of rock; opening it, he stepped inside, when, to his amazement, he found himself in an open plain, surrounded by high and inaccessible mountains, with over two hundred good houses, and many men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'We are called thieves,' was answered; 'but we only despoil the hated official class of some of their ill-gotten gains. No man can enter our stronghold and depart alive, unless he has become one of us; and to do so he must prove himself to be strong in body and mind.' Kil Tong consented to the conditions. Going up to a huge rock on which several men were seated, he laid hold of it and hurled it to some distance, to the dismay of the men, who fell from their seat, and to the surprised delight of all. He was at once installed a member, the contract sealed by mingling blood from the lips of all the members, and later made their chief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: On a given day Kil Tong, dressed in the red gown of a youth just betrothed, covered himself with the dust of travel and mounted on a donkey made his way to a large and strong Buddhist temple, well patronized by officials who made it a place of retirement for pleasure and debauch. He presented a letter to the head priest, stating that a train of one hundred ponies loaded with rice had been sent as a present from his father; the priests were delighted, and a great feast was ordered. Suddenly Kil Tong clapped his hand over his cheek with a cry of pain, and produced from his mouth a pebble, previously introduced on the sly: 'Is it to feed on stones that my father sent me to this place?' The priests bowed their shaven heads to the floor in humiliation, and at a sign from Kil Tong the robbers who had entered as grooms and in the rice bags seized servants and priests alike, loading the ponies with jewels, rice, cash and whatever of value they could lay hands upon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: An old priest made off quietly to the yamen and called for soldiers. Kil Tong, disguised as a priest, called to them to follow him down a by-path after the robbers; while he conveyed the soldiers over the rough path, the robbers made good their escape by the main road, leaving the soldiers groping helplessly in the dark among the rocks and trees in a direction opposite that taken by the robbers. Kil Tong's name was noised abroad, and the robber band made him their chief with the consent of all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Eight Kil Tongs, the Palace Cloud, and the Stork of the Garden

region.en: Royal palace, Seoul; islands off the west coast (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Novel tale (c. 1600s) collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 9, eBook #55539

summary.en: The audacity multiplies: the Pochang who boasted he would capture the robber alone is drugged at the stronghold and carried in a bag to a high mountain overlooking the capital, where he casts himself down; reports come of great depredations in each of the eight provinces at the same time, and when the orders are obeyed, a guard comes from each province bringing Kil Tong — eight men alike in every respect, each with the scar on the left thigh, and all found to be figures in straw and wax. A letter on the Palace gate offers to stop the depredations if the government confers the rank of Pansa; when Kil Tong comes to make his bow before the King, the assassins waiting are confounded — he is caught up in a cloud and borne away amid strange music. Later, in the royal gardens under a full moon, a flute sounds and a man descends seated upon the back of a gracefully moving stork: 'Fear not, O King. I am simply Hong Pansa. I have come to make my obeisance before your august presence and be confirmed in my rank.' Asking only three thousand bags of rice, he sails to an island off the west coast, founds a settlement, and the story turns on the rescue of a stolen lady from savage mountain bandits, whom he slays with the aid of his old friends the spirits (quay sin).
summary.zh: 捕頭自誇能擒吉童，反被藥啞，囊載至御苑山上，慚而投崖。未幾八道同時報警，朝廷按名捕拿，八道各解一人至，形貌無異，皆曰腿有瘢，驗之，乃稻草蠟人所為。吉童乃投書闕下，乞除參判之職即罷掠。入朝之際，忽乘雲而去，眾皆愕然。後於御苑月夜，自騎鶴而降，再拜請罪，乞米三千石，浮海而西，據島為王。山中遇劫掠民女之野人，以毒箭誅其酋，復召神兵（鬼神）盡殲其黨，遂娶所救之女。

passages.text: The Pochang, who had charge of the prisons and was a man of great courage, boasted he would capture the thief alone. Disguised as a traveller he fell in at a little inn with Kil Tong in disguise, was guided into the mountains and the stone-door stronghold, drugged with wine, and put into a bag and conveyed in a marvellous manner to a high mountain overlooking the capital; not daring to face his sovereign with such a fabulous tale, he cast himself down and was picked up dead in the morning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Simultaneous reports of great depredations came in each of the eight provinces, all attributed to Kil Tong. Official orders were issued to each of the eight governors; the orders were so well obeyed that upon a certain day soon after, a guard came from each province bringing Kil Tong, and there in a line stood eight men alike in every respect. Asked to decide which was his true son, the father stated that his son had a scar on the left thigh — instantly each of the eight men pulled up the baggy trousers and displayed a scar. When the guard was commanded to kill all of them, the men were found to be only figures in straw and wax.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: A letter posted on the Palace gate announced that if the government would confer upon Kil Tong the rank of Pansa, thus removing the stigma attaching to him as the son of a slave, he would stop his depredations. The decree was issued; but knowing the plans laid for him, as he passed through the gates and came near enough to be seen of the King, he was caught up in a cloud and borne away amid strange music, wholly discomfiting his enemies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some time after, the King was walking with eunuchs and attendants in the royal gardens, the leaves blood-red on the maples, when all were astonished by the sound of a flute played by some one up above them. Looking up among the tree-tops a man was seen descending toward them, seated upon the back of a gracefully moving stork. 'Fear not, O King. I am simply Hong Pansa. I have come to make my obeisance before your august presence and be confirmed in my rank.' 'I wish to go to a distant land, and settle down to the pursuit of peace and happiness. If I may be granted three thousand bags of rice I will gladly go and trouble you no longer.' In the early morning a fleet of junks appeared off the royal granaries, took on the rice, and made away before the people were well aware of their presence; Kil Tong sailed for an island off the west coast, and with his followers founded a settlement there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 9 (1889); not verbatim.
